feedback: If a learner ploughs left to right or stalls, prompt: 'Is there a pair that makes a ten, or a fact you already know?' Then let them try pairing 2 and 5.
If they doubt that reordering is allowed, have them compute two orders (e.g. 2 × 7 × 5 and 5 × 2 × 7) and confirm both give 70.
When they verbalise the chosen strategy ('I'll pair the 2 and 5 to make 10'), affirm that naming the plan is the skill being built.
activities.intendedInsight: Reordering factors is always allowed (commutativity/associativity) and the total stays the same — but some orderings turn a fiddly three-number product into a single known fact, so it pays to look for the friendly pair before calculating.
learnerActions: Work out 2 × 7 × 5 in your head, saying aloud which two numbers you multiply first and why.
Try pairing 2 and 5 first to make 10, then multiply by 7 to get 70; compare this with going left to right (2 × 7 = 14, then × 5 = 70).
Check that different orders give the same total: is 2 × 7 × 5 the same as 5 × 2 × 7? Explain why you are allowed to reorder.
Repeat with 2 × 9 × 5 and 4 × 3 × 5, each time scanning for a pair that makes a ten or a known fact first.
activities.title: Reorder three factors to find the easy pair

feedback: If a learner says 8 × 0 = 8 or 8 × 1 = 0, act it out with counters: 8 groups of 0 is nothing (0); 8 groups of 1 is 8. Contrast directly with adding 0.

If a learner expects ×1 to make the number bigger (believing multiplication always increases a number), use the single-group picture: one group of 8 is still 8, so multiplying by 1 changes nothing — multiplication does not always make a number larger.

If they confuse ÷1 with halving or with ÷0, return to the division picture: 8 ÷ 1 is one whole group (or groups of one), so you get everything back, 8. ÷0 is different — you cannot share 8 among zero groups, and no number of groups of 0 makes 8, so it is left undefined and out of scope.
Praise explanations that reference groups rather than restating a rule.
activities.intendedInsight: ×1 and ÷1 leave a number unchanged because you have one whole group (or share into groups of one), and ×0 gives 0 because there are no groups (or every group is empty) — these are meanings to be seen, not rules to memorise.
learnerActions: Lay out counters to show 8 × 1 as 'one group of 8' and '8 groups of 1'; confirm both give 8.
Show 8 × 0 as '8 groups of nothing' — every group is empty, so the total is 0.
Show 8 ÷ 1 as one whole group of 8 (or sharing 8 into groups of one) and confirm the result is still 8.
Say in your own words why n × 1 = n, why n × 0 = 0, and why n ÷ 1 = n.
Contrast 8 × 0 with 8 + 0: adding 0 leaves 8, but 0 groups of 8 (or 8 groups of 0) is nothing — notice the roles are different.
activities.title: Understand ×1, ×0 and ÷1 through groups

feedback: If a learner answers 24 (ten times too small), prompt: '4 what times 6? Four tens — so 24 tens, which is 240.'
Have them restate the known fact (4 × 6 = 24) and then re-apply the ten-times adjustment rather than reteaching from scratch when the method is sound but the number slips.
activities.intendedInsight: A known fact can be scaled by place value: 40 × 6 is ten times 4 × 6, so the answer is 240, not 24 — keeping the 'tens' label attached prevents losing the place value.
learnerActions: Work out 40 × 6 mentally by reasoning '4 tens × 6 = 24 tens = 240'; say the 'tens' name aloud as you go.
Explain how knowing 4 × 6 = 24 helps you get 40 × 6.
Try 30 × 7 and 50 × 8 the same way, keeping the place-value name attached to each digit.
Check your answer is sensible: 40 × 6 is exactly ten times 4 × 6, so 240, not 24.
activities.title: Scale with place value for multiples of ten

feedback: For a correct strategy with an arithmetic slip, do not reteach — ask the learner to re-state the known fact and re-apply the adjustment.
If explanations fall back on rules, redirect to the groups picture or to checking that two orderings give the same total.
Watch for the persistent 7 × 0 = 7 and 7 × 1 = 0 confusions and address them with counters (7 groups of 0 is 0; 7 groups of 1 is 7).
activities.intendedInsight: Strategy choice and the special-case results are things you can state and justify, not just compute — being able to explain why confirms genuine understanding.
learnerActions: Decide which pair you would multiply first in 2 × 9 × 5 and say why.
Give the results for 7 × 0, 7 × 1 and 7 ÷ 1, and explain each using the groups meaning.
Answer: why does any number × 1 equal that same number?
Explain why you are free to reorder the factors in a three-number product.
activities.title: Consolidate and check reasoning
